notes: Prompt 5 goals, durations, demonstration and reserve thresholds are provisional teaching choices, not NASA facts. Normal job timers are unchanged.

missions.question: What makes the solar meter rise?
missions.lesson: Panels turn sunlight into electricity. Packed panels must be installed first.
hints: Look at sunlight and the solar meter.
Install a solar array, then observe daylight.
Open Build and install Solar Array. Start and advance the mission; generation must cover habitat power.
advice: Engineer: install a panel before advancing time.
Scientist: compare daylight with generation.
Medic: keep habitat power running.

missions.question: What powers the base at night?
missions.lesson: Extra daylight energy charges batteries. Night uses that stored energy.
hints: Where can daylight energy wait?
Install enough panels and batteries. Charge them in preparation.
Use preparation steps to charge storage before a full cycle. Keep the marked reserve throughout; expand storage if night uses too much.
advice: Engineer: batteries store energy; they do not make it.
Scientist: compare charging and discharging.
Medic: preserve the reserve.

missions.question: Which load must stay powered?
missions.lesson: Protect essential power first. Turning a heater off saves energy but makes the habitat colder.
hints: Which load protects the crew?
Review loads before switching.
Keep habitat power on. Compare generation, demand and temperature before advancing.
advice: Engineer: habitat power cannot be switched off.
Scientist: optional loads have consequences.
Medic: a cold habitat is not a safe saving.

missions.question: Why does a dusty panel make less power?
missions.lesson: Settling dust reduces panel output. Compare with a clean-panel estimate and plan maintenance.
hints: Look for the sand-coloured coating.
Compare actual output with the clean-panel estimate.
Identify dust as the cause. Assign maintenance with a free astronaut; prepare storage before the next storm.
advice: Engineer: inspect the coating before maintenance.
Scientist: compare panels under the same sunlight.
Medic: preserve power while investigating.

missions.question: What helps when a storm reduces sunlight?
missions.answer: Charged batteries and careful load choices
missions.lesson: Prepare before storms. Cleaning removes panel dust, not dust in the sky. This compressed storm is a game profile.
hints: Mission Control warns before the storm.
Charge batteries and choose which loads can wait.
Store enough energy for the forecast. Cleaning needs a free Engineer and power; protect habitat power.
advice: Engineer: cleaning needs a free Engineer and power.
Scientist: NASA examples are not this game's forecast.
Medic: preserve essential power throughout.

missions.question: What does a working greenhouse need?
missions.answer: Electrical power as well as construction
missions.alternative: Only a packed greenhouse in cargo
missions.lesson: Powered greenhouses contribute food and oxygen but add a load. They do not automatically meet all crew needs.
hints: Packed equipment cannot grow food.
Build the greenhouse and check its lights and power cost.
While building, review forecasts, charge storage or consult crew. Then power the installed greenhouse and observe food production.
advice: Engineer: construction and power both matter.
Scientist: research is optional for this mission.
Medic: plants help, but the crew still uses reserves.

missions.question: How should we judge our oxygen supply?
missions.answer: Compare production, crew use and reserve
missions.alternative: Assume one greenhouse meets every need
missions.lesson: Crew use oxygen during simulation. Production can help without replacing all consumption; preserve a reserve.
hints: Compare production and consumption.
Crew size changes use. Plants make a contribution.
Keep oxygen above the marked reserve. Review storage, greenhouse power and optional research before starting.
advice: Engineer: capacity is not production.
Scientist: compare rates in matching units.
Medic: preserve reserves even when plants produce.
